structured_output.hypothesis: In the global fossil record, the Jaccard similarity of marine genus lists falls as the time gap between two stratigraphic stages grows, so adjacent stages share far more genera than stages that are widely separated.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Using PBDB marine animal genus occurrences binned by International Chronostratigraphic Chart stage, the median Jaccard similarity of genus sets for consecutive stage pairs (lag 1) is at least 2 times the median for pairs separated by 10 or more stages (lag >= 10). The Spearman correlation between lag and similarity is also at most -0.5 (p < 0.01). For the intermediacy part, for at least 75% of stage triplets (i, i+1, i+2) the middle stage's similarity to each neighbour exceeds the similarity between the two outer stages.
structured_output.fail_criterion: The median lag-1 Jaccard similarity is less than 1.5 times the median lag >= 10 similarity, or the Spearman correlation between lag and similarity is above -0.3. Alternatively, fewer than 60% of triplets show the middle stage as intermediate. Any of these refutes the claim. Values between the pass and fail thresholds count as inconclusive.
structured_output.interpretation: Darwin's 'formations' are mapped to the standard chronostratigraphic stages. A stage is used as a proxy because a formation is a local rock unit and a stage is a time unit. Darwin's 'fossils ... closely related' is operationalised as taxonomic overlap at genus level (Jaccard index of genera). This is a modern reinterpretation, because Darwin meant affinity at species, genus and family level. 'Remote' formations are stages 10 or more stages apart. 'Intermediate' means the middle stage's fauna overlaps both neighbours more than the neighbours overlap each other. Sampling standardisation (for example, restricting to genera with at least 10 occurrences and subsampling to equal occurrence counts per stage) is applied to avoid confounding by sampling effort. Fields used: accepted_name or genus, early_interval, late_interval, max_ma, min_ma, phylum, class.

dataset.why_it_fits: PBDB holds global fossil occurrences with taxonomic identification and numeric age bounds. The public data service (https://paleobiodb.org/data1.2/) returns occurrence lists as CSV or JSON, so genus-by-stage presence matrices can be built and tested for similarity decay with time gap.
